cultivar: Qing Xin Oolong, Si Ji Chun, Jin Xuan
processing: Light-oxidation, half-ball-rolled oolong made in a baozhong-derived way, on the low hills of Mingjian.
harvest_season: Mingjian is a lowland area with a long picking season; Si Ji Chun in particular is harvested repeatedly through the year.
appearance_dry: Dark-green half-rolled leaf with a light scent.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden-yellow, typical of lightly oxidised Taiwanese oolong.
appearance_wet: Green medium-sized leaves that open out, typical of the class.
taste_profile: Records say little beyond a light fragrance. Lightly oxidised lowland oolongs of this kind are typically floral and easygoing, with less depth than high-mountain tea.

brewing.notes: Everyday tea: keep the steeps short if it runs a bit brisk, as lowland oolongs can.

vintage_note: Usually sold fresh from the current year, as is normal for lightly oxidised Taiwanese oolong, and in large volume as an everyday tea. Much of Mingjian's output now goes as Si Ji Chun base tea for hand-shaken drinks, so a named Songbai Changqing packet is the smaller part of the market.
description:
Songbai Changqing, the Pine Cypress Evergreen tea, comes from the Songboling plateau in Mingjian, Nantou, at the south end of the Bagua hills. It is a low-altitude tea, grown at just over 500 metres on red soil, in a big area of gardens that is one of the island's main sources of everyday tea.

The gardens grow Qing Xin Oolong, Si Ji Chun and Jin Xuan, and the tea is made as a half-rolled, lightly oxidised leaf. That places it close to high-mountain tea in form, but the warmer lowland growing conditions make a lighter and simpler cup.

Don't expect mountain-tea density. As with other lowland oolongs, the appeal is an easy floral sweetness at a modest price, and it is a sensible tea for daily pots. Water just off the boil works, with short steeps if it starts to feel brisk.

The label can be a bit loose: Songboling, Mingjian and Songbai Changqing all point to the same area. Check the cultivar and the harvest; the best Si Ji Chun from here is a different drink from the base tea sent to bubble-tea shops.
history:
Tea growing in Mingjian is traced to the late Qing, when a Wang family from Anxi is said to have brought in oolong stock. The tea was known as Puzhong or Songbaikeng tea.

Its present name came from Chiang Ching-kuo, then premier, who tasted it on a visit in the 1970s and renamed it; accounts differ on the year, with 1973, 1975 and 1978 all given. Mingjian later became a major supplier of Si Ji Chun base tea for the drinks trade.
